problems.stem: What makes a biological material 'hierarchical' in the engineering sense?
options: It only operates at the atomic scale
Its performance emerges from coordinated structure across multiple scales
It contains no interfaces between layers
It is always softer than synthetic materials
problems.explanation: Hierarchical materials derive performance from organized structure at several scales, from microstructure up to visible form.

problems.stem: Why is nacre often used as a reference model for tough composites?
options: Because it is a perfectly homogeneous crystal
Because layered platelets and interfaces help deflect and slow cracks
Because it depends only on high density
Because it prevents any deformation from occurring
problems.explanation: Nacre's layered architecture and interfaces make crack growth more difficult, increasing toughness.

problems.stem: A collagen-inspired composite would most likely emphasize which design feature?
options: Single-scale uniformity with no orientation control
Multiscale fiber organization and load sharing
problems.explanation: Collagen systems organize fibers across scales so that loads can be distributed and redirected rather than concentrated.

problems.stem: Which engineering decision best reflects multiscale biomimetic thinking?
options: Optimizing only the outer shape while ignoring internal interfaces
Designing microstructure, mesostructure, and macro-form to work together
Choosing the hardest possible material and ignoring assembly
Replacing all interfaces with a fully uniform block
problems.explanation: Multiscale design treats performance as the product of coordinated structure across several levels, not one level alone.
